subtype: Approach: experiment and measure on resume versions [Revision]
passage:
Hi Seema,
Update on the job hunt: two weeks of silence, so I stopped guessing and ran a small experiment. I made two versions of my resume. Version A leads with my marks and college. Version B leads with my three projects, and the marks sit at the bottom. I sent each to twelve similar junior roles over ten days and tracked them in a sheet. A got one callback. B got five. It's a small sample, so I won't claim it proves everything, but it is enough for me to make B my default and test the summary line next. Thank you for suggesting I measure instead of worrying. Can I send you the third version when it's ready?
Best,
Rukmini

qa.q: How many callbacks did version B get?
How does Rukmini feel about the result?
qa.a: Rukmini feels encouraged but cautious, since it is a small sample and not proof of everything.
Rukmini could test the summary line, as planned, changing one thing at a time so the result is clear.

qa.q: How might Seema feel reading the update?
qa.a: Seema is probably pleased, since the suggestion to measure instead of worrying paid off.

grounding: After two silent weeks, the student tries two resume versions, tracks callbacks and finds the one leading with projects does better than the one leading with marks.

subtype: Approach: experiment and measure on resume versions [Revision]
passage: Avni, you asked what changed after my two silent weeks. I ran an experiment on myself. I'm Abhinav, the stats nerd, so of course I did. I made two resumes. Version A opened with my CGPA, 8.1, and my school marks. Version B opened with two projects: the bus-tracking app our team built for the college shuttle, and a small inventory tool I wrote for my uncle's shop. Everything else was the same. Over the next three weeks I sent twenty applications with A and twenty with B, similar roles, same days of the week. I logged it all in a sheet. A got one callback. B got six. Six! Nobody at those companies cared much about my Class 12 marks. They wanted to see something I'd built. I deleted Version A that same night. Best forty applications I've ever sent.

qa.q: How many callbacks did Version B get?
How did Abhinav feel when the numbers came in?
qa.a: Abhinav was excited and surprised, repeating six, and glad to finally have clear evidence.

qa.q: What else could Abhinav test next?
qa.a: Abhinav could test two ways of describing the projects, or two cover notes, changing one thing at a time to keep improving.

qa.q: How might Avni see the experiment?
qa.a: Avni, who asked what changed, gets a simple method to try with Avni's own resume.

grounding: Shows a student testing two resume versions after silent weeks, tracking callbacks, and finding the project-first version beats the marks-first one.

subtype: Approach: experiment and measure on resume versions [Revision]
passage: I'm Uma, and I share a flat with Ritu, so I watched her resume experiment from the sofa. After two weeks of silence, she printed two versions and stuck them side by side on the fridge. The left one opened with her marks: "CGPA 8.4, university rank 12." The right one opened with "Projects": a water-usage dashboard for our housing society and a translation tool she'd built for her grandmother. She sent fifteen applications with each, alternating, and kept a tally on a sticky note under each page. By the end of the month, the left page had two ticks. The right page had seven. Ritu stood in front of the fridge for a long moment. Then she pulled the left page down, folded it, and put it in the recycling. I can't say exactly what she felt, but she hummed while cooking that night.

qa.q: How many applications did Ritu send with each version?
qa.a: Ritu sent fifteen applications with each.

qa.q: What might Ritu have felt standing at the fridge?
qa.a: Ritu may have felt surprised and pleased, even relieved, since the projects version clearly won and she hummed while cooking that night.

qa.q: What else could Ritu do with the winning version?
qa.a: Ritu could tailor the projects section for each role, putting the most relevant project first.

qa.q: How does Uma see the experiment?
qa.a: Uma watches it from the sofa and reads Ritu's mood from small signs like the humming, without claiming to know exactly what Ritu felt.

grounding: Illustrates a student trying two resume versions, tallying callbacks, and seeing that the project-first version outperforms the marks-first one.
